scenes.title: Where Demand Meets Supply
scenes.summary:
Move the sliders and touch why a liter of gasoline costs what it costs.

When the price rises, people want to buy less and sellers want to sell more. The point where the two amounts match is the equilibrium. There, nobody has a reason to change the price. The two amount formulas sit side by side below.

For example, when a 🍬 candy costs 300 won, all 30 🧑 classmates fight to buy one. At 1,000 won, nobody buys any. The 🏪 shop owner puts out more candy the higher the price goes. The market stops at the price where the two amounts match.

scenes.title: Splitting the Lunch Budget
scenes.summary:
Split a 40-won lunch budget between gimbap and tteokbokki, then find the best combo.

The 💰 money you can spend is fixed. What you spend on the two foods cannot pass the budget. The best combo is where the last won buys the same happiness on either food. The second formula below states that condition.

For example, you have 4,000 won: a 🍞 bread costs 1,000 and a 🥛 milk costs 2,000. One of each fits the budget exactly. If the last 100 won on bread felt better, buy less milk and one more bread.

scenes.title: The Cafe Owner's Math
scenes.summary:
Open a cafe and work out how many cups to sell to come out ahead.

The cost of one more cup of ☕ coffee is the marginal cost. It climbs as the cups pile up. While the price beats that cost, each sale adds profit. Stop where the two become equal — that rule is the formula below.

For example, a cup costs 2,000 won to make and sells for 4,500, so each cup adds 2,500. By evening, ingredients run low and one more cup costs 5,000. From then on, every extra cup loses 500 won.

scenes.title: Competition vs Monopoly
scenes.summary:
Put the same market side by side: competition on the left, monopoly on the right.

With competition, many 🏪 shops pull the price down toward cost. A monopolist stops where marginal revenue meets marginal cost. Fewer trades happen, and the lost gains stay as a red triangle. The less price-sensitive customers are, the bigger that triangle grows.

For example, if one video app is the only one your 🧑 classmates watch, a fee hike leaves them nowhere to go. With three similar apps, one hike sends everyone elsewhere. The more trapped the customers, the bigger the monopolist's triangle.

scenes.title: Taxes and Price Ceilings
scenes.summary:
Put a tax on cigarettes and a cap on rent, then see who actually pays.

A tax drives a wedge between the price buyers pay and the price sellers get. The wedge lands heavier on the side that cannot walk away. A price ceiling freezes the price but makes buyers line up instead. The formula below splits the tax burden.

For example, add a 100-won tax to one 🍬 candy. A 🧑 classmate who cannot live without candy pays almost all of the higher price. A classmate who can take it or leave it just stops buying. Then the 🏪 shop cuts its own price and shoulders the tax.

scenes.title: Two Firms Watching Each Other
scenes.summary:
In a town with only two cola firms, each firm sizes up the other and picks its output.

The price is set by the two firms' combined output. Once the rival picks a quantity, a reply rule gives your best answer. The market settles where the two replies cross. That reply rule is the formula below.

For example, only two booths sell 🍬 candy at the school fair. If the other booth puts out 10 📦 boxes, your share shrinks. If it puts out fewer boxes, you can add more without sinking the price.

scenes.title: The Factory and the River
scenes.summary:
Waste flows into a river upstream, and the fishing village downstream pays for it.

A 🏭 factory counts only its own cost. Society's true cost adds the damage done to the river. The market hears only the factory's cost and produces too much. A tax sized to the damage closes the gap. The cost-adding formula is below.

For example, the upstream village dumps trash in the river, so 🧑 kids downstream cannot swim in it. The dumpers pay nothing, so they keep dumping. Charge a fine for each bag of trash, and the dumping shrinks.

scenes.title: Tragedy of the Shared Pasture
scenes.summary:
Everyone grazes sheep on one shared pasture — watch why no grass survives.

The pasture belongs to everyone; the sheep belong to each herder. The more sheep there are, the less grass each one eats. Still, each 🧑 herder counts only the profit from their own animals. So the total overshoots the right flock size, and the pasture's profit evaporates. The right size is in the formula below.

For example, a class 📦 box holds 30 🍬 candies. Take just one a day and they last a whole month. If everyone grabs handfuls, the box is empty in three days. One simple rule — at most two each — keeps the candies alive.

scenes.title: Why Does the Superstar Earn So Much?
scenes.summary:
A star singer's fee and land near a station split the same way — see why both are so high.

The payment for a factor splits into two parts. What it could earn in its next job is transfer earnings. The pure bonus above that is economic rent. The harder a factor is to replace, the more of its pay hardens into rent. The formula below ties that to a steep supply.

For example, a 🧑 singer nobody can replace gets a fee of 1,000,000 won. A karaoke singing job would pay only 100,000. The other 900,000 is pure rent. If that voice were common, the fee would sink toward 100,000.

scenes.title: The Amusement Park Pricing Puzzle
scenes.summary:
Sell the same ride three ways: per ride, a flat pass, and a two-part tariff.

Per-ride pricing charges like a monopolist and cuts use. A flat pass makes extra rides free, so guests overuse them. A two-part tariff splits the bill into an entry fee and a per-ride price. Price rides at cost and collect the leftover gain at the gate, and the waste vanishes. The payment formula is below.

For example, running one ride costs the park 500 won. At 3,000 won a ride, 🧑 kids ride only twice. A 5,000-won entry fee plus 500 won a ride makes five rides feel fine. The park pockets its gain in the entry fee.

scenes.title: Three Ways to Tax
scenes.summary:
Run one market under three taxes: lump-sum, specific, and ad valorem.

A lump-sum tax is a fixed bill, so it never enters the price decision. Trade stays untouched. A specific tax drives a fixed wedge into every unit sold. An ad valorem tax widens the wedge by a share of the price. Only wedged taxes shrink trade and leave a loss triangle. The two wedge formulas are below.

For example, three taxes visit a 🍬 candy shop. The lump-sum tax is 10,000 won a month, sold or not. The specific tax takes 100 won per candy. The ad valorem tax takes 10 percent of the price. Only the per-candy taxes raise the price and shrink how many get bought.

scenes.title: Why Higher Prices Mean Buying Less — Except When They Don't
scenes.summary:
Split the response to a price rise into the two forces that drive it.

The substitution effect pulls you away from the pricier good. The income effect is the feeling of a thinner wallet. Usually the two push the same way. For an inferior good, the income effect pushes back. For a survival staple like rice, it can win, so a higher price means buying more. The formula below adds the two forces.

For example, a 10,000-won allowance buys 🍚 rice and 🍌 bananas. When rice gets pricier, bananas look cheap and you switch toward them. At the same time your allowance feels smaller, so you buy less overall. If rice matters too much to cut, you drop the bananas and buy even more rice.

scenes.title: Why Good Used Cars Never Show Up
scenes.summary:
See why good used cars never show up on the market.

Only the seller knows the quality. Buyers set their price by the average of whatever shows up. A low average makes good-car owners give up selling. So the average sinks further, and the price spirals down to zero. The same structure wears three faces: hidden quality, adverse selection, and moral hazard. In health insurance, healthy people leave first and premiums climb again. Banks trusting deposit insurance turn reckless after the deal. The average-quality formula is below.

For example, a 🧑 classmate offers a used game console for 50,000 won. Only the seller knows whether it is broken. The nervous buyer offers just 30,000. Owners of working consoles will not sell at that price. Only the broken ones stay on the market.

scenes.title: Winning the Auction, Losing Money
scenes.summary:
See why the winner of a coin-jar auction ends up the biggest loser.

Each bidder's guess scatters around the true value. The winner is whoever guessed the highest. More bidders means the top guess puffs up even further. Winning itself is the news that you overestimated the most. The formula below sizes that puff.

For example, a jar holds 100 🍬 candies, and 10 🧑 classmates each guess the count. One classmate guesses 130 and bids the highest, so they win. Inside are only 100, a loss equal to the 30-candy overcount.

scenes.title: Preference Relations and Axioms
scenes.summary:
This scene draws your preferences on the two-good plane.

A ranking is rational when nothing is left unranked. It also never loops back on itself. Such a ranking can be written as utility numbers, as in the formula below. Change the utility family and the whole curve map changes. You also see what breaks when an axiom fails.

For example, suppose a 🍎 apple bundle beats a 🍌 banana bundle. And the banana bundle beats a 🍞 bread bundle. Then the apple bundle must beat the bread bundle too.

scenes.title: Choice Rules and WARP
scenes.summary:
In this scene you pick bundles yourself under two different budgets.

A chosen bundle reveals what you like. A bundle you could afford but skipped counts as worse. If two situations flip each other's picks, that is a contradiction. The formula below, WARP, is the rule that catches it.

For example, you have 💰 1,000 won and pick 🍎 apples, though 🍌 bananas cost no more. The next day you pick bananas, though apples cost no more. Your two picks now contradict each other.

scenes.title: The Budget Set
scenes.summary:
Draw the region of bundles you can afford, set by prices and your money.

If the two goods together cost more than your money, that bundle is out. The borderline is the budget line. When one good gets pricier, the line rotates inward. With more money, the line shifts outward in parallel. The budget set and slope formulas are below.

For example, a 6,000-won allowance buys 🍎 apples at 1,000 won each and 🍌 bananas at 2,000 won each. Apples alone, you can get six; bananas alone, three. If apples rise to 2,000 won, only three apples fit the budget.

scenes.title: Walrasian Demand and the Demand Curve
scenes.summary:
Draw a demand curve from Cobb-Douglas tastes, then scale prices and money together.

Demand spends a fixed share of the budget on the good. A higher price buys less with that share, sliding you along the curve. Scaling prices and money by the same factor leaves every affordable bundle unchanged. So demand stays put — that sameness is the homogeneity formula below.

For example, half of a 10,000-won allowance always goes to 🍞 bread. At 1,000 won a loaf, that buys five loaves. At 2,000 won, it buys only two and a half. Double both the allowance and the price, and you are back to five.

scenes.title: Indifference Curves and MRS
scenes.summary:
This scene draws the indifference map of Cobb-Douglas utility.

An indifference curve joins bundles that feel equally good. Move the reference bundle and the whole map redraws. The marginal rate of substitution is the tangent slope there, as in the formula below. It says how much of one good replaces one unit of the other.

For example, giving up one 🍎 apple feels fine if you get two more 🍌 bananas. Then the MRS is two. The fewer apples you have, the more each apple is worth.

scenes.title: Utility Maximization
scenes.summary:
This scene finds the best bundle where the budget line meets an indifference curve.

The optimum is where the budget line just touches the curve. Move prices or wealth and the optimum slides along. At that spot the MRS always equals the price ratio, as in the formula below. You can check it numerically at every moment.

For example, you have 💰 6,000 won for 🍎 apples and 🍌 bananas, each 1,000 won. If you like both equally, three apples and three bananas are best. If apples get pricier, you buy fewer apples and more bananas.

scenes.title: The Slutsky Decomposition
scenes.summary:
This scene splits a price rise into two effects to see why demand falls.

A price change brings two effects at once. The substitution effect pushes you away from the pricier good. The income effect comes from feeling poorer than before. You can compensate by the old bundle or by the old utility. The two ways split the formula below differently.

For example, if 🍎 apples get pricier, switching to 🍌 bananas is the substitution effect. If you then buy less fruit overall because 💰 money feels tight, that is the income effect.

scenes.title: Expenditure Minimization and Duality
scenes.summary:
This scene finds the cheapest way to reach a target utility.

Now the problem runs in reverse. Fix the satisfaction level first, then shrink the cost. The cheapest bundle sits where an isocost line touches the curve. Turn on the mirror and it lands exactly on the earlier optimum. Two problems mirroring each other is duality.

For example, you want the satisfaction of 🍞 bread, two slices, and 🥛 milk, one glass. You shop for that satisfaction at the lowest cost. To save 💰 money, you shift toward the cheaper good.

scenes.title: Aggregating Demand
scenes.summary:
This scene adds three consumers into one demand. Stack their curves together and the market curve appears.

Some properties survive the adding-up. If everyone spends their whole budget, so does the market. Double every price and income together, and demand stays put. Move each person's curve and check for yourself.

For example, three 🧑 classmates buy 🍎 apples. The first buys 2, the second 3, the third 5. Together the class buys 10 apples. If prices and 💰 allowances all double, the count stays the same.

scenes.title: The Representative Consumer
scenes.summary:
This scene asks whether many people can act as one. Shuffle money between two people with identical tastes.

However the money is split, aggregate demand never moves. What one person loses, the other gains exactly. Only the total amount of money matters. Then a representative consumer exists. The whole market computes like one imaginary person.

For example, twin brothers split a 💰 allowance of 12,000 won. The older may take 8,000 and the younger 4,000. Swap the split, and the 🍎 apples they buy stay the same. Only the total matters, not who holds what.

scenes.title: Isoquants
scenes.summary:
This scene draws the isoquant map of a production function.

An isoquant joins input mixes that make the same output. Move the reference input point and the tangent slope changes. That slope is the marginal rate of technical substitution below. It says how much of one input replaces a unit of the other.

For example, one fewer 🧑 worker plus one more ⚙️ machine still bakes 100 🍞 bread rolls. The scarcer workers get, the more each worker is worth.

scenes.title: Cost Minimization
scenes.summary:
This scene finds the cheapest input mix for a target output.

The cheapest mix is where the isoquant touches an isocost line. When a factor price changes, that spot slides. You use less of the pricier input and more of the cheaper one. The lowest cost then becomes the cost function below.

For example, baking 100 🍞 bread loaves, 💵 wages rise but ⚙️ machine prices stay put. The cheapest mix then uses fewer 🧑 workers and more machines.

scenes.title: Cost Curves
scenes.summary:
This scene pulls marginal and average cost curves out of a total cost curve.

Marginal cost is the extra cost of making one more unit. Average cost is total cost divided by quantity. When one more unit costs less than the average, the average falls. So the marginal cost curve passes exactly through the lowest point of average cost.

For example, a 🏪 shop's average cost is 1,000 won per 🍞 bread loaf. Baking one more costs 800 won, so the average falls. At 1,200 won, the average rises instead. That is why marginal cost meets average cost at its lowest point.

scenes.title: Expected Utility
scenes.summary:
See how to score a lottery. Give each outcome a happiness score, weight it by probability, and add up.

The key: 💰 money does not pile up happiness at a steady rate. The richer you are, the less one more coin delights you. So the average prize, paid for sure, feels better than the gamble itself. That difference is the Jensen gap.

For example, flip a coin: heads pays 100 won, tails pays nothing. The average prize is 50 won. But offer a sure 40 won instead, and many friends pick the 40. The sure thing is easier on the heart.

scenes.title: Measuring Risk Aversion
scenes.summary:
See how to put a number on fear of risk. One slider makes the fear bigger or smaller.

The bigger the fear, the more the sure thing is worth. A gamble averaging 50 won gets sold for a sure 💰 money of 30 won. The 20 won shaved off is the risk premium. The 📏 ruler that measures this fear is the formula below.

For example, one friend quits a coin-flip game right away for a sure 30 won. Another friend holds out for 45 won. The second friend is simply less afraid.

scenes.title: Demand for Insurance
scenes.summary:
Compare two versions of life in one picture: sick and healthy. Insurance is a promise that fattens your share in the bad case.

At a fair premium, covering the bad case completely is best. Both cases end up holding the same 💰 money. Add a loading to the premium and the math changes. Covering only part of the loss becomes the smarter deal.

For example, 30 🧑 classmates each chip in 100 won every month. When someone gets hurt, the pot helps pay the hospital bill. If nobody gets hurt, the 100 won is simply gone. Still, the hurt friend is spared a scary bill.

scenes.title: Normal-Form Games and Best Responses
scenes.summary:
Look directly at the two-player payoff table. Each of the four cells lists both players' payoffs.

In each column, mark the first player's best answer. In each row, mark the second player's best answer. The cell where both marks land gets a star. That cell is a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Neither player wants to move away alone.

For example, say you and a 🧑 friend each pick heads or tails on a coin. If your friend picks heads, one answer is best for you. Your pick likewise settles your friend's best answer. The pairing where both answers point at each other is the equilibrium.

scenes.title: Mixed Strategies and the Indifference Condition
scenes.summary:
Watch the second player mix two strategies by probability. Slide the mixing probability back and forth.

As the rival's mix changes, my expected payoff from each strategy moves along a straight line. At the mix where the two lines cross, neither strategy is better. Only that indifferent mix can appear in a mixed equilibrium. Making your rival indifferent is what pins down your mix.

For example, say a 🧑 friend takes a penalty kick with a ⚽ ball against a goalkeeper friend. Always kicking left lets the keeper guard only left. So the kicker mixes left and right kicks. The mix makes the keeper equally unhappy guarding either side.

scenes.title: Zero-Sum Games and Minimax
scenes.summary:
Look at a game where one player's gain is exactly the other's loss. Edit the payoff numbers yourself.

I try to make my worst case as good as possible. My rival tries to make my gains as small as possible. When the two calculations agree, a saddle point appears and the equilibrium is pure. When they disagree, both players must mix, and the game gets a value as in the formula below.

For example, bet one 🍬 candy on guessing heads or tails of a coin. Guess right and the candy is yours. Guess wrong and your 🧑 friend takes it. Whatever you win, your friend loses. So both of you mix to stay unreadable.

scenes.title: Nash Equilibrium and Best-Response Correspondences
scenes.summary:
Draw both players' best-response curves on one plane. The blue curve and the orange curve appear together.

The blue curve is my best answer to the rival's mixing probability. The orange curve is the best answer in the other direction. Where they cross, each is a best response to the other. That crossing is a Nash equilibrium. Pure equilibria sit at the corners, and the mixed one is starred inside.

For example, say you and a 🧑 friend each choose left or right. Your best answer changes with your friend's choice. Your friend's best answer changes with yours too. The pairing where both answers fit each other is the equilibrium.

scenes.title: Iterated Elimination of Strictly Dominated Strategies
scenes.summary:
Watch dominated strategies get deleted one by one. Push the round slider to eliminate them in order.

If a strategy always does worse than another one, no rational player uses it. Delete it and the table shrinks. In the smaller table, another bad strategy shows up. In this scene C, M, and D vanish in turn until only U remains.

For example, say a 🏪 shop sells three kinds of 🍬 candy. One kind is always smaller and less tasty than another kind. Nobody ever picks it, so it can leave the shelf. Once it is gone, another always-worse candy stands out. Deleting step by step leaves the final choice.

scenes.title: Extensive-Form Games and Backward Induction
scenes.summary:
Draw the entry game as a tree. The order of moves is visible at a glance.

Solve it by reading backwards from the end. First fix the last mover's best answer. Knowing that answer settles the earlier player's choice too. A threat to fight is not credible, because fighting hurts the threatener once entry happens. So that branch gets pruned away.

For example, say a neighborhood has one snack 🏪 shop and a new one wants to open. The old owner threatens a price war. But once the new shop opens, fighting costs the old owner too. The newcomer knows this and enters anyway.

scenes.title: Repeated Games and Cooperation
scenes.summary:
Watch the Prisoner's Dilemma repeated forever. The strategy punishes any betrayal forever.

Betray today and you gain a lot right now. But from tomorrow your partner betrays too, and the losses keep coming. How much you care about tomorrow decides the choice. Care enough about the future, and cooperation pays and holds. The boundary value comes from the formula below.

For example, say you and a 🧑 friend take turns lending a ⚽ ball every day. Hog the ball today and today is fun. But from tomorrow your friend never lends it to you. If you want to keep playing together, keeping today's promise wins.

scenes.title: Supply, Demand, and Equilibrium
scenes.summary:
The competitive equilibrium is where the demand and supply curves cross. That crossing fixes both price and quantity at once.

Now add a per-unit tax and a wedge opens up. The price buyers pay pulls apart from the price sellers receive. Fewer trades happen, and the lost trades destroy welfare. That destroyed part is the deadweight loss in the formula below. What remains splits into consumer surplus, producer surplus, and tax revenue.

For example, say a 🍬 candy sells for 100 won at the corner 🏪 shop. A tax of 20 won per candy makes shoppers pay 110 won while the shop keeps only 90. The 20 won in the middle is the wedge. Pricier candy means fewer friends buy it.

scenes.title: Tax vs Quota: Deadweight Loss
scenes.summary:
A tax and a quota are different policy tools. Yet both shrink the amount traded.

Switch the tool and the lost welfare keeps the same shape. The deadweight-loss triangle holds its area either way. Only the destination of the transfer changes. With a tax it becomes government revenue. With a quota it becomes rent for whoever holds the quota.

For example, say the corner 🏪 shop sells 10 🍬 candies a day. The government caps sales at 6 a day, so 4 trades vanish. Some friends who wanted candy cannot buy it. That frustration over vanished trades is the deadweight loss. The shop holding the selling permit pockets the rent instead.

scenes.title: Externalities and the Pigouvian Tax
scenes.summary:
The factory's cost and the neighborhood's cost come apart here.

The factory counts only its own cost.
It never counts the harm from its smoke.
Social cost adds the two together, as in the formula below.
So the factory produces too much, thinking it is cheap.
The lost welfare is the red triangle.
Flip the Pigouvian tax on, and the cost curve aims at the social optimum.

For example, a 🏭 factory makes one toy for 100 won.
Its chimney smoke dirties the neighbor's laundry.
That damage is worth 30 won.
The true cost is 130 won, but the factory counts only 100.
So it makes too many toys.

scenes.title: Public Goods and Free-Riding
scenes.summary:
Everyone uses the same public good, but who pays to provide it?
Public-good demands add up vertically, not horizontally.

Everyone consumes the same unit at the same time.
So willingness to pay is stacked vertically.
Where that sum meets the cost is the optimum.
But each person reasons differently.
Hoping others will pay, each pays nothing.
Too little is collected, so supply falls short.

For example, 30 🧑 classmates chip in to buy a ⚽ ball for the classroom.
The ball costs 30,000 won.
If half think 'the others will pay' and pay nothing, the money falls short.
Nobody gets a ball to play with.

scenes.title: Monopoly: Marginal Revenue and Deadweight Loss
scenes.summary:
Look at a market with only one seller. That single firm chooses price and quantity alone.

The monopolist slides down the demand curve to set the price. Selling one more unit means cutting the price, so marginal revenue falls twice as fast as demand. It stops where marginal revenue meets marginal cost. Producing less than competition leaves welfare destroyed. That triangle is the deadweight loss. The markup over cost is measured by the Lerner index below.

For example, say the neighborhood has exactly one snack 🏪 shop. The owner sets the price of tteokbokki alone. Charge too much and friends stop buying. Charging a bit more and selling less can still raise profit. But the friends who go without feel the loss. That loss is the deadweight loss.

scenes.title: Cournot Oligopoly
scenes.summary:
Two firms compete while watching each other's output. Each picks its best quantity against the other.

My best quantity depends on how much my rival makes. That relationship is the reaction function. Where the two reaction functions cross sits the Cournot-Nash equilibrium. Add more firms and price and quantity move toward competition. With just one firm, it is monopoly again.

For example, say the neighborhood has two snack 🏪 shops. If one makes lots of tteokbokki, the other does better making little. Watching each other, they settle on quantities that stop moving. Grow to ten shops, and the price falls close to cost.

scenes.title: Price Discrimination
scenes.summary:
Watch the art of charging different prices for the same good. Switch between uniform pricing, third-degree, and first-degree discrimination.

Third-degree splits buyers into markets and matches marginal revenue to marginal cost in each. First-degree charges each buyer exactly their willingness to pay and turns all surplus into profit. Surprisingly, third-degree can destroy more welfare than one uniform price. Splitting markets is not always more efficient.

For example, say a stationery 🏪 shop sells ✏️ pencils. The owner charges a regular 🧑 friend 100 won but a first-time visitor 150. The friend buys happily at the low price, and the owner earns more overall. Each customer faces a different price tag.

scenes.title: The Edgeworth Box and Competitive Equilibrium
scenes.summary:
The box holds everything two people own. Endowments, offer curves, and the contract curve all appear in one picture.

The contract curve collects points where neither person can do better without hurting the other. At the equilibrium price, one budget line touches both indifference curves at once. That tangency is the competitive equilibrium. The thick part of the curve is the core, which no one can block.

For example, say you hold 7 🍎 apples and 3 🍌 bananas. Your 🧑 friend holds 7 bananas and 3 apples. You like bananas more, and your friend likes apples more. Trading makes both of you happier. When no trade helps anymore, you land on a point of the contract curve.

scenes.title: The Two Welfare Theorems
scenes.summary:
Walk along the utility possibility frontier. Pick a point with the slider and move it around.

The competitive equilibrium always sits on the frontier. That is the First Welfare Theorem. Other points on the frontier are reachable too. Support the point with the right price and shift income in one lump sum. Then the market lands there by itself. That is the Second Theorem, and the formula below gives the transfer.

For example, say you and a 🧑 friend split 10 🍬 candies. Every split that uses all 10 is efficient. But if your friend's share feels too small, there is a fix. Hand a few candies to your friend before trading starts. Then plain market trading reaches the split you wanted.

scenes.title: Tatonnement Dynamics
scenes.summary:
Watch an auctioneer hunt for equilibrium by calling out prices. Each call compares demand with supply, then moves the price.

If 🧑 people queue up to buy, the price goes up. If goods pile up unsold, the price goes down. Small careful steps land right on the equilibrium. Huge hasty steps overshoot and drift away. The formula below is exactly this adjustment rule.

For example, a 🏪 shop owner rewrites the 🍎 apple price tag every day. Sold out means the price goes up; rotting leftovers mean it goes down. Raise it all at once and every customer walks away. Nudge it little by little and the right price appears.

scenes.title: Excess Demand: Existence and Uniqueness
scenes.summary:
Measure how much extra people want at each price and draw it as a curve. Where the curve crosses zero is the equilibrium.

A positive excess means buyers want more than sellers offer. A negative excess means the opposite. In a well-behaved economy the curve crosses zero exactly once. But that is a gift, not a guarantee. Switch the mode and you can watch it cross three times.

For example, call out 🍞 bread prices from 100 up to 1,000 won. Priced too cheap, 🧑 people line up to buy. Priced too dear, loaves pile up unsold. Only at the right price is there no line and no leftovers. That price is the equilibrium.

scenes.title: Shrinking of the Core (Debreu–Scarf)
scenes.summary:
Copy the same economy and grow its scale. Watch the divisions everyone accepts narrow down to one.

When the economy is small, a few agents can break away and do better alone. As 🧑 people multiply, those escape routes get sliced away. Exactly one division survives in the end. It is the very division the market picks. The core shrinks to a point, as in the formula below.

For example, splitting 10 🍎 apples between 2 friends, almost any split works. Grow the group to 100 friends and the story changes. Unhappy friends can team up and cook up a new split. In the end only one split survives — one nobody can break away from.

scenes.title: Blocking Coalitions
scenes.summary:
Drag the division around and watch who objects. If some group can object, the division falls.

If one 🧑 person ends up worse than going alone, that person walks out. If a group can split things better together, it falls too. Only divisions nobody can walk away from survive. That surviving set is the core.

For example, three friends split 10 🍬 candies. If one friend gets only 1 candy, that friend walks away. If two friends secretly find a better split, the original split collapses. Only a split nobody wants to leave stays standing.

scenes.title: Arrow–Debreu Equilibrium
scenes.summary:
An Edgeworth box for consumption in each state.
Two people share each other's risk here.

With no risk for the whole economy, they insure each other.
Both consume exactly the same in every state.
That is full insurance, the mutuality principle.
When the whole economy shakes, everyone shakes together.

For example, Minsu grows 🍎 apples and Jihoon grows 🍌 bananas.
If only Minsu's harvest fails, Jihoon shares.
If only Jihoon's fails, Minsu shares.
Both eat the same every year.
But if the whole country's harvest fails, there is nothing to share.

scenes.title: State Prices and Scarcity
scenes.summary:
Three states, with probabilities and state prices side by side.

A state price is not a raw probability.
It is a probability weighted by marginal utility.
A dollar in the scarcest state costs the most.
The formula below shows exactly that weighting.

For example, a village usually has plenty of 🍞 bread.
In a famine year, bread is very scarce.
Money to spend in that year is worth far more than money in a normal year.

scenes.title: Intertemporal Equilibrium and the Interest Rate
scenes.summary:
Watch a market that trades today's share against tomorrow's share. The interest rate is the price of that swap.

A 🧑 person with plenty today lends the spare share out. A person short today borrows, spends now, and repays tomorrow. The rate settles where the borrowing meets the lending. The formula below is the exchange rate between today's 💰 money and tomorrow's.

For example, one friend receives the full 10,000 won allowance this month. She lends 5,000 won to a friend who is short this month. Next month she receives 5,500 won back, interest included. The lender spends less today and the borrower spends more.

scenes.title: Overlapping Generations and the Golden Rule
scenes.summary:
See life in generations: earn while young, spend while old. The young generation and the old never actually meet.

The young generation has plenty and the old generation has little. Their lifetimes never overlap, so they cannot trade directly. 💰 Money builds the bridge between them. The young trade goods for money, and spend that money when old.

For example, a grandfather sold 🍚 rice for money when he was young. Now old, he buys rice from a young farmer with that money. When that farmer grows old, he will buy from the next generation. This is how money links the generations.

scenes.title: Arrow's Theorem
scenes.summary:
This scene stress-tests rules that merge many rankings into one. Switch profiles and rules and watch what breaks.

Majority rule can spin in a circle. A beats B, and B beats C. Then C turns around and beats A. The Borda count wobbles for another reason. Delete a hopeless alternative and the ranking flips. No rule keeps all four fairness conditions.

For example, three 🧑 friends run for class president. The class splits into three groups with clashing favorites. Head to head, A beats B and B beats C. Yet C beats A. Majority rule alone cannot pick a president.

scenes.title: Social Welfare Functions
scenes.summary:
This scene merges two people's happiness into one score. It picks the best among all possible happiness pairs.

One slider changes how the merging works. Count only the sum, and the bigger total wins. Hate inequality more, and the score changes. At the extreme, only the worse-off person counts. The best point slides toward the equal diagonal. The formula below fixes the merging rule.

For example, two 🧑 friends split 15 🍬 candies. One friend gets 9 and the other gets 6. Judged by the sum alone, this split scores best. Care more about fairness, and they split 7.5 each. The worse-off friend's happiness sets the score.

scenes.title: The Value of Information
scenes.summary:
Should you invest or not? A signal helps you decide.

The more accurate the signal, the better the decision.
After seeing the signal, you recompute the probability.
A good signal says invest.
A bad signal says stop.
The value of information is the gap between deciding with it and without it.
The formula below pins that gap down.

For example, before buying a used 🚗 car, you ask an expert.
The expert spots good and bad cars correctly 80 percent of the time.
If the expert says good, you buy.
If the expert says bad, you walk away.
Your losses shrink a lot.

scenes.title: Optimal Sequential Search
scenes.summary:
You visit shops one by one, hunting for the best price.

Each extra shop costs you money.
So you set one cutoff value in advance.
An offer better than the cutoff, you buy at once.
An offer worse than the cutoff, you keep looking.
That cutoff is the reservation value in the formula below.

For example, you shop around for a 👕 shirt.
Each extra shop costs 1,000 won in 🚌 bus fare.
You decide in advance: under 50,000 won, I buy immediately.
At 60,000 won you walk out.
At 48,000 won you buy on the spot.

scenes.title: Akerlof's Lemons Market
scenes.summary:
Good cars vanish from a used-car market.

Only the seller knows the car's quality.
The buyer sets the price by the average.
At an average price, good-car owners refuse to sell.
Only bad cars remain, so the price falls further.
As the price unravels like this, trade itself disappears.

For example, there are 10 used 🚗 cars.
A good one is worth 10 million won.
A bad one is worth 1 million won.
The buyer cannot tell them apart and offers the average, 5.5 million.
Then every good-car owner walks away.
Seeing only bad cars left, the buyer lowers the price again.

scenes.title: Education Signaling
scenes.summary:
When skill cannot be shown directly, a diploma speaks instead.

Studying is easier for the able worker.
So only the able can afford the costly degree.
For the less able, copying is just too painful.
Firms read the diploma and guess the skill.
Yet the education itself builds no skill.
So the signaling cost below is pure waste.

For example, a fast 🧑 runner easily wins a race medal.
A slow runner can hardly win one at all.
So a medal tells everyone who is fast.
But winning the medal makes nobody faster.

scenes.title: Screening Menus
scenes.summary:
A seller lays out a menu, and buyers pick for themselves.

The seller cannot tell big spenders from small ones.
So the menu offers two sizes.
The big option is made in full.
The small option is shrunk on purpose.
Shrinking it stops big spenders from lying.
In return, big spenders pocket a bonus called information rent.
The formulas below set the two sizes.

For example, a 🏪 shop sells 🍬 candy in a big 📦 box and a small box.
Big spenders choose the big box.
The small box is made tiny on purpose.
Pretending to be a small buyer would only hurt.
So big spenders honestly pick the big box.

scenes.title: Moral Hazard and Incentives
scenes.summary:
This scene designs a contract when the boss cannot watch the work. A flat wage alone gives no reason to work hard.

Pay must hang on the outcome. Good results need a bonus on top. Two conditions must hold at once. Working hard must beat slacking off. And the job must be worth taking at all. The less the worker fears risk, the gentler the bonus slope. It is a tug-of-war between sharing risk and pushing effort.

For example, you run a 🏪 snack shop and leave a part-timer alone. You cannot see how hard they work. So you do not fix the wage. On days the shop earns more 💰 money, you pay a bonus. Then the part-timer works hard on their own.

scenes.title: Which Effort to Implement
scenes.summary:
This scene asks whether high effort is worth buying. Making someone work hard is never free.

As the effort cost rises, the profit from high effort falls. The profit from low effort stays flat. Where the two profits meet is the cutoff. Incentives pay only on the cheap side of it. The effort cost is exactly the risk premium you must cover.

For example, a parent sets the 💰 allowance for an errand. A trip to the nearby 🏪 shop takes 1,000 won. A far shop is tiring and needs more. If the price gets too high, going in person is cheaper. Hard effort is worth buying only while it stays cheap.

scenes.title: The Revelation Principle and Optimal Auctions
scenes.summary:
This scene finds the best rule for selling one item. We skip complicated games and only ask directly.

The revelation principle says honest rules are enough. Ask the buyer what the item is truly worth. Reports below the reserve get nothing. Reports at or above it pay exactly the reserve. A well-chosen reserve maximizes expected revenue. The virtual value in the formula below marks the spot.

For example, you sell one ⚽ soccer ball. Your friend values it at 8,000 won. You set the reserve at 5,000 won. If your friend reports at least 5,000, the ball is theirs. They pay exactly 5,000 💰 won. Lying gains nothing, so honesty wins.

scenes.title: Second-Price Auction: Truth-Telling Is Dominant
scenes.summary:
This scene shows why honest bidding wins in a second-price auction. There is one opponent, and they bid honestly.

Your bid does not set the price you pay. Winning means paying the opponent's bid. So bidding above your value gains nothing. It only creates wins that cost too much. Bidding lower throws away wins you could afford. As the formula below shows, the loss grows with the square of the gap.

For example, your class auctions off one ⚽ ball. You value it at 6,000 won. A friend bids 4,000 won. Bid your honest 6,000 and you win. You pay only the friend's 4,000 💰 won. Bid 8,000 and the price stays the same. But if the friend had bid 7,000, you would overpay.

scenes.title: Maskin Monotonicity
scenes.summary:
This scene tests whether a desired rule can arise as a game's equilibrium. Two people choose among three options.

The test is called Maskin monotonicity. Suppose some option wins in one situation. In another situation, that option has fallen for nobody. If the rule then picks something else, it fails. No game can ever implement such a rule. A dictator rule passes the test. The pick-the-bottom rule gets a red violation.

For example, your class votes on what to play. This week ⚽ soccer wins. Next week nobody has soured on soccer. If the result suddenly flips to 📚 reading, the rule is fishy. Such a rule cannot come from any fair game.

terms.definition: How many percent quantity changes when price changes by 1\% — a gauge of responsiveness. Steeper curves are more elastic.
The boundary of affordable bundles with income m — p_1x_1 + p_2x_2 = m. The happiest point on this line is the choice.
A binary relation \succsim on a set X of alternatives. x \succsim y means the consumer likes x at least as much as y. A rational preference is complete and transitive.
The axiom that for any two alternatives x, y, either x \succsim y or y \succsim x (or both) holds — the consumer can compare any pair.
The axiom that x \succsim y and y \succsim z imply x \succsim z — it guarantees the consistency of preferences.
x \sim y when x \succsim y and y \succsim x both hold — the two alternatives are equally good.
A function u: X \to \mathbb{R} representing \succsim: x \succsim y \iff u(x) \ge u(y). Any monotone transform represents the same preference, so it is an ordinal concept.
A rule assigning to each budget set (a subset of feasible alternatives) B the set C(B) \subseteq B of alternatives actually chosen.
The consistency condition: if x is chosen when y was available, then x must not be available whenever y is chosen. Choice derived from rational preferences satisfies WARP.
The set of affordable consumption bundles at prices p and wealth w: B_{p,w} = \{x \ge 0 : p \cdot x \le w\}. Its boundary is the budget line.
Under locally nonsatiated preferences the optimum spends the whole budget: p \cdot x = w. If money were left over, a better bundle would be affordable.
The good serving as the price standard — its price is normalized to 1. Demand is unaffected by the numeraire choice thanks to homogeneity in prices and wealth.
The solution x(p, w) of the utility maximization problem — demand as a function of prices and wealth. Also called Marshallian demand.
terms.sceneTitle: Walrasian Demand and the Demand Curve

terms.definition: Walrasian demand is homogeneous of degree zero in prices and wealth: x(\alpha p, \alpha w) = x(p, w). A proportional rise in all prices and income changes nothing real.
terms.sceneTitle: Walrasian Demand and the Demand Curve

terms.definition: The set \{x : u(x) = \bar{u}\} of bundles yielding equal utility. Under monotonicity and convexity it slopes downward and is convex to the origin.

The slope (in absolute value) of an indifference curve — how much of good 1 the consumer needs at the margin to give up one unit of good 2. MRS = \frac{\partial u / \partial x_1}{\partial u / \partial x_2}.
\max_x u(x) subject to p \cdot x \le w. Its solution is Walrasian (Marshallian) demand x(p, w); its value is indirect utility v(p, w).
The value function of the UMP, v(p, w) = \max_{p \cdot x \le w} u(x). Nonincreasing in prices, nondecreasing in wealth, homogeneous of degree zero.
The formula recovering Walrasian demand from indirect utility: x_l(p, w) = -\frac{\partial v / \partial p_l}{\partial v / \partial w}.

Decomposes a price effect into substitution and income effects: \frac{\partial x_l}{\partial p_k} = \frac{\partial h_l}{\partial p_k} - \frac{\partial x_l}{\partial w} x_k. The substitution effect is always nonpositive.
The effect of a price change on demand holding utility compensated — the slope of Hicksian demand. Always nonpositive for the own price.
The effect of a price change on demand through changed real purchasing power. Same direction as the substitution effect for normal goods, opposite for inferior goods.
The solution h(p, u) of the expenditure minimization problem — the cheapest bundle achieving utility u. Homogeneous of degree zero in prices, nonincreasing in own price.
A good whose demand rises when its price rises — happens when a strong inferior-good income effect overwhelms the substitution effect.
\min_x p \cdot x subject to u(x) \ge u. Its solution is Hicksian demand h(p, u); its value is the expenditure function e(p, u).
The value function of the EMP, e(p, u). Homogeneous of degree one in prices, concave, nondecreasing — and yields Hicksian demand via Shephard's lemma.
Differentiating the expenditure function in a price gives Hicksian demand: h_l(p, u) = \frac{\partial e(p, u)}{\partial p_l}.
The UMP and EMP mirror each other: h(p, u) = x(p, e(p, u)), x(p, w) = h(p, v(p, w)). Each problem's solution recovers the other's.
The sum of individual demands X(p) = \sum_i x^i(p, w_i). Walras' law and homogeneity of degree zero survive aggregation, but WARP generally does not.
A fictional consumer whose demand reproduces aggregate demand. Exists (independently of the wealth distribution) when indirect utilities take the Gorman form.
v_i(p, w_i) = a_i(p) + b(p) w_i — indirect utility with a common marginal utility of wealth b(p). Makes aggregate demand depend only on total wealth.
The set \{(z_1, z_2) : f(z_1, z_2) = q\} of input bundles producing output q. Convex to the origin when the production function is concave.
The slope (in absolute value) of an isoquant — how much of input 1 marginally replaces one unit of input 2 holding output fixed. MRTS = \frac{\partial f / \partial z_1}{\partial f / \partial z_2}.
How output scales when all inputs scale by t: increasing if f(tz) > t f(z), constant if equal, decreasing if smaller.
The solution z(w, q) of the cost minimization problem — the inputs chosen at factor prices w to produce target output q.
c(w, q) = \min_{f(z) \ge q} w \cdot z — the minimum cost of producing q. Homogeneous of degree one in factor prices, concave, nondecreasing.
The extra cost of making one more unit — discretely MC = \Delta C / \Delta q, continuously MC(q) = c'(q). Profit maximization sets price equal to marginal cost, pinning down supply.
AC(q) = c(q)/q — cost per unit. The marginal cost curve passes through the minimum of the average cost curve.
A probability distribution over outcomes C — the mathematical form of an uncertain prospect. A simple lottery puts probabilities on finitely many outcomes.
The utility of a lottery U(L) = \sum_n p_n u(x_n) — the expectation of Bernoulli utility u. Under continuity and independence, preferences take this form.
If L \succsim L' then \alpha L + (1-\alpha)L'' \succsim \alpha L' + (1-\alpha)L'' for any L'' and \alpha \in (0,1) — a common mixture never reverses the ranking. The Allais paradox breaks it.
Preferring a sure amount over a lottery with the same expected value — equivalent to a concave Bernoulli utility u.
The sure amount c indifferent to lottery L: u(c) = \mathbb{E}[u(L)]. For a risk averter, c < \mathbb{E}[L].
\pi = \mathbb{E}[L] - c — the slice of expected value the agent would give up to avoid the lottery. The price of risk aversion.
The coefficient of absolute risk aversion r_A(x) = -u''(x)/u'(x) — a local gauge of how strongly risk is disliked.
A premium equal to the expected loss — zero expected profit for the insurer. At a fair premium, a risk averter buys full insurance.
A strategy profile where no player can gain by unilaterally deviating, holding others' strategies fixed. Each strategy is a best response to the rest.
A strategy that randomizes over pure strategies. In equilibrium every pure strategy in the mix yields the same expected payoff (the indifference condition).
terms.sceneTitle: Mixed Strategies and the Indifference Condition

terms.definition: A strategy that is best no matter what others do. Iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies (IEDS) simplifies a game but can miss Nash equilibria.
terms.sceneTitle: Iterated Elimination of Strictly Dominated Strategies

terms.definition: A strategy profile that is a Nash equilibrium in every subgame. It rules out non-credible threats and is found by backward induction.
The gap between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay — the triangle under demand and above price.
Total surplus destroyed when quantity deviates from the efficient level (taxes, monopoly) — measured by the Harberger triangle.
A tax that corrects an externality — setting \tau = MD(Q_s) equal to marginal damage brings the market back to the social optimum.
Non-rival, non-excludable goods. The Samuelson condition (vertical sum of marginal benefits = marginal cost) sets optimal supply, but free-riding causes underprovision.
A single seller maximizing profit at MR = MC — price exceeds marginal cost and deadweight loss arises.
terms.sceneTitle: Monopoly: Marginal Revenue and Deadweight Loss

terms.definition: An oligopoly model where firms choose quantities simultaneously. Reaction functions intersect at the Cournot-Nash equilibrium, converging to competition as the number of firms grows.
A box plotting two consumers' endowments and indifference curves together. Points on the contract curve are Pareto efficient allocations.
terms.sceneTitle: The Edgeworth Box and Competitive Equilibrium

terms.definition: A state where no one can be made better off without making someone worse off. The First Welfare Theorem says competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient.
The set of allocations no coalition can profitably block. In a replica economy the core shrinks to competitive equilibrium as the economy grows (Debreu-Scarf).
Equilibrium with complete markets in state-contingent commodities. With no aggregate risk, full insurance (risk sharing) obtains.
No social welfare function satisfies universality, Pareto, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and non-dictatorship all at once.
Market unraveling when the informed side selects in — Akerlof's market for lemons is the canonical case.
Costly revelation of type by the informed side — Spence's education model yields a separating equilibrium.
The problem that the agent's post-contract action (effort) is unobservable. Risk sharing trades off against incentives under the incentive-compatibility constraint.
The condition that truth-telling is optimal for participants. By the revelation principle, design can be restricted to direct mechanisms.
terms.sceneTitle: The Revelation Principle and Optimal Auctions

terms.definition: The second-price auction — bidding truthfully is a weakly dominant strategy. The canonical incentive-compatible mechanism.

exercises.statement: Gasoline demand is Q_d = 12 - P and supply is Q_s = 2P. Find the equilibrium price and quantity.
The lunch budget grows to m = 60. Food 1 costs p_1 = 6, food 2 costs p_2 = 8. What is the best bundle satisfying the budget equation p_1 x_1 + p_2 x_2 = m?
The cafe has fixed cost 20 and marginal cost MC = 4 + 2q. If the coffee price drops from P = 20 to 16, what happens to the best quantity and profit?

Two cola firms face the price P = 18 - (q_1 + q_2) and a cost of 3 per bottle. In the Cournot equilibrium, how much does each firm make and what is the price? Compare the total with monopoly and competition.
A star athlete's market has demand w = 18 - q and supply w = 6 + 2q. Find the payment w and quantity q, then split the total payment into economic rent and transfer earnings.

A gym member's visit demand is q = 16 - P and each visit costs the gym 2. If the gym prices visits at cost, 2, and lives off the membership fee alone, how many visits does the member make, and what is the most the gym can charge per month?
A consumer with a lunch budget of 40 and food 2 at 8 meets a half-price sale on food 1 (4 down to 2). How much does food 1 grow, and how does the increase split into substitution and income effects?
A tax t = 4 hits a market with demand Q_d = 10 - 0.5P and supply Q_s = P. How is the tax split between buyers and sellers, and how large is the deadweight loss?
A sheep is worth v(S) = 10 - S and costs 2. If the herders grow to 9, what happens to the total flock and the pasture's total profit? What per-herder limit would restore the optimum?

Shops in a market with demand P = 12 - Q and supply P = 2 + Q are charged a yearly license fee of 10 — a lump-sum tax. What are the quantity, revenue, and deadweight loss? Compare with a specific tax of t = 3, and explain what happens if the fee rises to 15.

In a used-car market, quality spreads evenly from 0 to 100 and buyers value a car at 1.6 times its quality (k = 1.6). Find the first price, the shrink factor per round, the number of cuts before the price falls below 10, and the gains from trade that vanish. How large must k be for the market to survive?
A consumer reports (5, 1) \succ (3, 3) and (3, 3) \succ (2, 4). If the preference relation \succsim is complete and transitive, what can be said about (5, 1) versus (2, 4)?

Consider a perfect-substitutes consumer with u(x_1, x_2) = x_1 + x_2. Find the marginal rate of substitution MRS = \frac{\partial u / \partial x_1}{\partial u / \partial x_2} and write the equation of the indifference curve through (6, 6). Is B = (9, 4) preferred to A = (6, 6)?
The consumer chose x = (20, 40) at (p, w) = ((1, 1), 60) and y = (25, 25) at (p', w') = ((3, 1), 100). Compute the revealed-preference relations and decide whether WARP is violated.

Pairwise choices over the three bundles A = (4, 4), B = (5, 2), C = (2, 5) came out as follows (each pair has a unique winner): A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. Prove that no complete and transitive preference relation \succsim rationalizes all three choices.
With p_1 = 2, p_2 = 1, w = 60, find the two intercepts and the slope of the budget line.
At p = (1, 1), w = 60 the bundle (30, 30) lies on the budget line. When p_1 rises to 2, is this bundle still affordable? Describe the geometric change of the budget line as well.
With u(x_1, x_2) = x_1^{1/4} x_2^{3/4}, p_1 = 2, p_2 = 1, w = 80, find x_1(p, w) and verify that doubling all prices and wealth leaves demand unchanged.
For \lambda > 0, prove that B(\lambda p, \lambda w) = B(p, w), and deduce directly from the definition of the UMP that Walrasian demand x(p, w) is homogeneous of degree zero.
With u(x_1, x_2) = x_1^{1/3} x_2^{2/3}, p_1 = 2, p_2 = 3, w = 120, find Walrasian demand x(p, w) and indirect utility v(p, w).
Starting from the budget line with p_1 = 1, p_2 = 2, w = 100, how does the budget line move when w rises to 150? Find the new optimum of a Cobb-Douglas consumer with a = 1/2.
Let u = x_1^{1/4} x_2^{3/4}, p_2 = 1, w = 80. When p_1 rises from 1 to 4, compute the substitution, income, and total effects of the Slutsky decomposition.
Prove directly from the definition of the EMP that the expenditure function e(p, u) is homogeneous of degree one in prices.
Prove with the Slutsky equation that a Giffen good cannot arise under Cobb-Douglas utility.
Prove the duality identity e(p, v(p, w)) = w from the definitions of the UMP and EMP (assume interior solutions and local nonsatiation).
Three Cobb-Douglas consumers have parameters a = (0.4, 0.5, 0.6), wealths w_i = 50, and p_2 = 1. At p_1 = 2, find each consumer's x_1^i and aggregate demand X_1.

Suppose each consumer i satisfies Walras' law p \cdot x^i(p, w_i) = w_i (no assumption on the functional form of demand). Prove that aggregate demand X(p) = \sum_i x^i(p, w_i) satisfies p \cdot X(p) = \sum_i w_i.

Two identical-taste Cobb-Douglas consumers with a = 1/2, total wealth W = 100, p_1 = 1, p_2 = 1. Compute X_1 for the splits s = 0.25 and s = 0.75, and verify that individual demands change while aggregate demand does not.

Suppose I consumers have indirect utilities of the Gorman form v_i(p, w_i) = \alpha_i(p) + b(p)\,w_i with a common b(p) > 0. Use Roy's identity to derive each demand, prove that aggregate demand X(p) depends only on total wealth W = \sum_i w_i, and exhibit a representative consumer's indirect utility reproducing it.
For the production function q = z_1^{1/3} z_2^{2/3}, compute the MRTS at (z_1, z_2) = (2, 8).
With w_1 = 3, w_2 = 1, q = 10, \alpha = \beta = 1/2, find the conditional factor demands z(w, q) and the minimum cost c(w, q).
For C(q) = 40 + 30q - 4q^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}q^3, find the output minimizing average variable cost and the marginal cost there.

Let \alpha = 0.3, \beta = 0.4 (decreasing returns), w_1 = w_2 = 1. Compute c(w, 16)/c(w, 8) from the conditional-demand formula, explain why it exceeds 2, and state the degree of homogeneity of c(w, q) in q in general.
A consumer with u(x) = \sqrt{x} evaluates a lottery paying 144 with probability 1/2 and 36 with probability 1/2. Find the certainty equivalent and the risk premium.
Show that in CRRA utility u(x) = x^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma), the (normalized) utility converges to log utility as \gamma \to 1: \lim_{\gamma \to 1} \frac{x^{1-\gamma} - 1}{1-\gamma} = \ln x.

A consumer with W = 100, loss L = 60 (probability \pi = 0.3), and u(x) = \sqrt{x} buys \beta coverage at premium rate p per dollar. Differentiate expected utility with respect to \beta to derive the first-order condition and solve for \beta^*(p). Check the value at p = 0.3.

Two CRRA consumers A (\gamma_A = 0.5) and B (\gamma_B = 2) evaluate the 50-50 lottery (150, 50). Compute each certainty equivalent and risk premium, and explain via the Arrow-Pratt measure who is more risk averse.
In the Prisoner's Dilemma \begin{matrix} & C & D \\ C & (3,3) & (0,5) \\ D & (5,0) & (1,1) \end{matrix}, find each player's strictly dominant strategy and the pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.

Find the fully mixed Nash equilibrium (p^*, q^*) of the Battle of the Sexes \begin{matrix} & O & F \\ O & (3,2) & (0,0) \\ F & (0,0) & (2,3) \end{matrix} and compute each player's equilibrium expected payoff.
For the zero-sum game \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix} (player 1's payoffs), find maximin and minimax, confirm no saddle point, then compute the mixed equilibrium and the value.
Prove that a 2 \times 2 zero-sum game with no pure-strategy saddle point has a unique fully mixed Nash equilibrium, and derive its value v = \frac{ad-bc}{a-b-c+d}.
Find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria of the Stag Hunt \begin{matrix} & S & H \\ S & (4,4) & (0,3) \\ H & (3,0) & (3,3) \end{matrix} and rank them by Pareto dominance.

In \begin{matrix} & L & C & R \\ U & (4,3) & (5,1) & (6,2) \\ M & (2,1) & (8,4) & (3,6) \\ D & (3,0) & (9,6) & (2,8) \end{matrix}, iteratively eliminate strictly dominated strategies and find the final outcome.
Show Matching Pennies \begin{matrix} & H & T \\ H & (1,-1) & (-1,1) \\ T & (-1,1) & (1,-1) \end{matrix} has no pure-strategy equilibrium, and find its unique (mixed) equilibrium.
Prove that the set of strategy profiles surviving iterated elimination of strictly dominated strategies contains every Nash equilibrium.
Find the subgame-perfect equilibrium of the entry game (Stay Out → (0,2); after Enter, Accommodate → (1,1), Fight → (-1,-1)) by backward induction.
Show that (Stay Out, Fight-if-enter) is a Nash equilibrium but not subgame perfect, and explain the difference between the concepts.

In the infinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with T = 4, R = 3, P = 1, find the minimum discount factor \delta^* for grim-trigger to sustain cooperation, and decide whether cooperation holds at \delta = 0.5.

Prove by backward induction that finitely repeating ( T times) a stage game with a unique pure-strategy Nash equilibrium has a unique subgame-perfect equilibrium: repeat the stage equilibrium every period.
In a market with demand P = 12 - Q and supply P = 4 + Q, find the competitive equilibrium (Q^*, P^*) and the consumer and producer surplus at it.
With demand P = 12 - Q and supply P = 4 + Q, a per-unit tax t = 3 is imposed. Find the deadweight loss and the tax revenue.
In the same market, find the deadweight loss of a quota \bar{Q} = 2, and the tax rate that gives the same deadweight loss.
In the linear supply-demand model, prove geometrically from the triangle that DWL = t^2/(2(B+D)), and explain why doubling the tax rate quadruples the deadweight loss.
With demand P = 10 - Q, MPC = 2 + Q, and MD = 1 + Q, write down the social marginal cost curve and find the social optimum Q_s.
With demand P = 10 - Q, MPC = 2 + Q, and MD = 1 + Q, find the Pigouvian tax rate and verify that the market quantity under that tax equals the social optimum.
For a public good with D_1: P = 12 - G, D_2: P = 6 - G, c = 4, find the voluntary-contribution Nash equilibrium (g_1, g_2) and the Samuelson optimum G^*, and compare them.

Suppose the two consumers have equal demand slopes (b_1 = b_2 = b). Express in terms of a_1, a_2, c the condition under which the voluntary-contribution Nash equilibrium falls short of the Samuelson optimum, and prove it.
With demand P = 14 - Q and c = 2, find the monopolist's profit-maximizing (Q_m, P_m) and its profit.
In a 3-firm Cournot market with demand P = 10 - Q and c = 2, find the symmetric Nash equilibrium per-firm output, total output, and price.
With n = 100 identical consumers each having demand P = 12 - q and c = 2, find the profit-maximizing two-part tariff (fixed fee F + per-unit price p).
In the Cournot equilibrium with linear demand P = A - BQ and N symmetric firms, prove that each firm's Lerner index \frac{P - c}{P} equals its market share divided by demand elasticity.
In an economy with a_1 = 1/3, a_2 = 2/3, W = (12, 12), e^1 = (9, 3), find the equilibrium price p_1 (with p_2 = 1).
Show that the endowment itself can be Pareto inefficient: with a_1 = a_2 = 1/2, W = (10, 10), e^1 = (9, 1), exhibit an allocation that strictly improves both consumers.
In the symmetric economy (a_1 = a_2 = 1/2, W = (10,10), e^1 = (7,3)), in which direction must the lump-sum transfer flow to decentralize the Pareto optimum x^1 = (4, 4)? Find its size.

Prove that the core always contains the competitive equilibrium. (Hint: suppose the equilibrium allocation x^* were outside the core — which coalition could block it? Consider that coalition's budget at equilibrium prices.)
In a market with D(p) = 36/p and S(p) = 2 + 2p, find the equilibrium price and determine whether tatonnement raises or lowers the price at p = 2.
Explain the intuition for why the gross substitutes condition \partial z_l / \partial p_k > 0 (l \ne k) implies uniqueness of equilibrium in a 2-good economy.
In an L-good economy, prove with Walras' law that if excess demand is zero in L-1 markets, it is zero in the remaining market too.
In a Cobb-Douglas exchange economy, show that z_1(p_1) \to +\infty as p_1 \to 0^+, and explain why this is the heart of the existence argument.
Explain via strict concavity why a core allocation in a replica economy satisfies "equal treatment" — i.e., same-type consumers get the same bundle.
In the symmetric economy with N = 2, show that coalition (2, 1)'s per-capita endowment is (17/3, 13/3), and explain the intuition for why it blocks x^1_1 = 5.42.
Explain (with this chapter's numerical example) that the core always contains the competitive allocation, but not conversely.
Discuss how the Debreu–Scarf theorem connects to the claim that "as the economy grows large, the price mechanism is justified."
With log utility, \pi_1 = 0.4, E_1 = 8, E_2 = 12, find the state price ratio q_1/q_2.
When both consumers' endowments are already fully insured (e^1 = (5, 5)) with no aggregate risk, show that no trade occurs in Arrow–Debreu equilibrium.
Discuss whether risk aversion \gamma affects state prices. (Hint: compare the log-utility formula with the \gamma \ne 1 case.)
In an economy with S states, L goods, and T dates, find how many contingent commodities an Arrow–Debreu equilibrium needs for complete markets, and give the number for S = 2, L = 2, T = 2.
With e^1 = (8, 2) and r = 0.5, find consumer 1's present-value budget set and give both intercepts of the budget line.
From 1 + r = E_2/(\delta E_1), explain what happens to the equilibrium interest rate when all consumers become more impatient (\delta falls).
In an OLG economy with \delta = 0.75, e = 12, find the steady-state savings rate s/e.
Explain what it means for money to be "essential" in the OLG economy, via the steady-state allocation.
For the mixed profile (1: A > B > C, 2: A > C > B, 3: B > A > C), find the Borda scores and the plurality outcome.
Explain why all four rules (Condorcet, Borda, plurality, dictator) satisfy the Pareto condition on the unanimous profile.
Explain how \rho in the CES social welfare function connects to inequality aversion, via the two extremes \rho = 1 and \rho \to -\infty.
Explain why Arrow's theorem does not mean "democracy is impossible", via what the conditions (U, P, IIA, D) exactly rule out.
With \pi = 1/2, signal accuracy q = 0.7, R = 120, L = 80, compute the value of information \text{VoI}.
Let X \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 100] and search cost c = 12.5. Find the reservation value r^* and the expected number of searches under the optimal policy, and verify V(r^*) = r^* by direct computation.
Prove that the value of information is always zero when signal accuracy is q = 1/2. Verify with the numerical example \pi = 0.4, R = 100, L = 60.
From the reservation-policy value V(r) = \frac{M+r}{2} - \frac{cM}{M-r} and the indifference condition c = \frac{(M-r^*)^2}{2M}, prove algebraically that V(r^*) = r^*.
In the lemons market with m = 1.5, suppose the current price is p = 0.8. Find the average quality of the cars offered, the buyer's willingness to pay, and the next-step price p_1.

In the signaling model with \theta_H = 2, \theta_L = 1, c(e,\theta) = e/\theta, show that e^* = 2 is also a separating equilibrium, and compare the size of the waste with the least-cost equilibrium e^* = 1.
In the screening model with \theta_H = 2, \theta_L = 1, \lambda = 0.95, find the optimal menu, show that the low type is excluded from the market, and compute the welfare loss.
When m < 2, show that the unraveling map f(p) = mp/2 is a contraction on [0, 1], and use this to prove that the unraveling process converges to p^* = 0 from any starting price.

With p_1 = 0.8, p_0 = 0.2, \bar u = 20, u(w) = w^{1/2}, c = 10, the optimal contract (w_L, w_H) = (277.78, 1111.11) is given. Compute the agent's expected utility under high effort and the payoff from shirking, and show the incentive-compatibility constraint holds with equality.
Prove with Jensen's inequality that the risk premium C_1 - (\bar u + c)^{1/\alpha} is always nonnegative. When does equality hold? Check with the numerical example \alpha = 1/2, c = 10.

Let \alpha = 1/2, p_1 = 0.8, p_0 = 0.2, x_H = 2000, x_L = 0, \bar u = 20. If the effort cost is c = 25, should the principal implement high effort or settle for low effort? Answer by computing both profits directly.

Prove that the threshold effort cost c^* increases in the risk-aversion parameter \alpha: the less the agent dislikes risk, the more expensive an effort the principal is willing to incentivize. Verify by direct computation that c^* = 1200 when \alpha = 1.
In the one-buyer auction with v \sim U[0,1], compute expected revenue at reserves r = 0.2 and r = 0.8, and compare each with the optimal reserve's revenue.
With reserve r = 0.5, what is the payoff of a buyer with value v = 0.4 who reports \hat{v} = 0.8? Compare with truth-telling and confirm in this example that the gain from lying cannot exceed zero.
My value is v = 70 and the opponent bids truthfully. If I bid b = 50, what are my expected payoff and win probability? Find the loss relative to truthful bidding.

Consider a symmetric auction with two bidders whose values are i.i.d. U[0,1]. Using that the optimal mechanism "sells to the bidder with the highest virtual value, only when that virtual value is nonnegative", show the optimal reserve is still r^* = 0.5 and compute the expected revenue.

The base profile \theta is agent 1: c \succ a \succ b, agent 2: a \succ b \succ c. Under perturbation 1 (agent 2: a \succ c \succ b), compute f_{\text{anti}}(\theta) and f_{\text{anti}}(\theta'), and confirm that x = c fell for neither agent.

Under the dictatorial rule f_{\text{dict}}, look at perturbation 4 (agent 1: a \succ c \succ b). Show that x = f_{\text{dict}}(\theta) fell for agent 1, and explain why this is still not a monotonicity violation.
Explain at the level of ideas — not a formal proof — why a social choice rule implementable in Nash equilibrium must satisfy Maskin monotonicity. Use the whistle-blower intuition.

Suppose f is fully implemented in Nash equilibrium by a mechanism \Gamma = (M, g). Let x = f(\theta), and suppose moving to \theta' the outcome x fell for no agent. Show that a Nash equilibrium m^* at \theta remains a Nash equilibrium at \theta', and conclude f(\theta') = x.
